source_text: Ἤδη μὲν οὖν τινες ἐπειράθησαν καὶ ὀνοματοποιίαις χρήσασθαι, ἵν', ὥσπερ διὰ καυτήρων τινῶν τῆς ἀσυνήθους καὶ ξένης ὀνομασίας, τὸ ἰδίωμα ἑκάστου γένους ἐπιγινώσκηται. Καὶ τὰ μὲν ὠνόμασαν σχιζόπτερα, ὡς τοὺς ἀετούς· τὰ δὲ δερμόπτερα, ὡς τὰς νυκτερίδας· τὰ δὲ πτιλωτὰ, ὡς τοὺς σφῆκας· τὰ δὲ κολεόπτερα, ὡς τοὺς κανθάρους, καὶ ὅσα ἐν θήκαις τισὶ καὶ περιβολαῖς γεννηθέντα, περιρραγέντος αὐτοῖς τοῦ ἐλύτρου, πρὸς τὴν πτῆσιν ἠλευθερώθη. Ἀλλ' ἡμῖν ἀρκοῦσα σημείωσις πρὸς τὴν τῶν γενῶν ἰδιότητα ἡ κοινὴ χρῆσις, καὶ οἱ παρὰ τῆς Γραφῆς περί τε καθαρῶν καὶ ἀκαθάρτων διορισμοί. Ἄλλο μὲν οὖν γένος τὸ τῶν σαρκοφάγων, καὶ ἄλλη κατασκευὴ πρέπουσα τῷ τρόπῳ τῆς διαίτης αὐτῶν, ὀνύχων ἀκμαὶ, καὶ χεῖλος ἀγκύλον, καὶ πτερὸν ὀξὺ, ὥστε καὶ συλληφθῆναι ῥᾳδίως τὸ θήραμα, καὶ διασπα ραγὲν τροφὴν τῷ ἑλόντι γενέσθαι. Ἄλλη τῶν σπερμολόγων κατασκευή· ἄλλη τῶν ἐκ παντὸς τρεφομένων τοῦ συν τυχόντος. Καὶ ἐν τούτοις πλεῖσται διαφοραί. Τὰ μὲν γὰρ αὐτῶν ἐστιν ἀγελικὰ, πλὴν τῶν ἁρπακτικῶν· τούτων δὲ οὐδὲν κοινωνικὸν ἐκτὸς τοῦ κατὰ τὰς συζυγίας συνδυασμοῦ. Μυρία δὲ ἄλλα τὸν ἀθροισματικὸν ᾕρηται βίον, ὡς περιστεραὶ, καὶ γέρανοι, καὶ ψῆρες, καὶ κολοιοί. Πάλιν ἐν τούτοις τὰ μὲν ἄναρχά ἐστι καὶ οἷον αὐτόνομα· τὰ δὲ ὑφ' ἡγεμόνι τετάχθαι καταδεχόμενα, ὡς αἱ γέρανοι. Ἤδη δέ τις καὶ ἑτέρα ἐν τούτοις ἐστὶ διαφορὰ, καθ' ἣν τὰ μὲν ἐπιδημητικά τέ ἐστι καὶ ἐγχώρια, τὰ δὲ ἀπαίρειν πέφυκε πορροτάτω, καὶ χειμῶνος ἐγγίζοντος ἐκτοπίζειν ὡς τὰ πολλά. Χειροήθη δὲ καὶ τιθασσὰ τὰ πολλὰ τῶν ὀρνέων ἐκτρεφόμενα γίνεται, πλήν γε δὴ τῶν ἀσθενῶν, ἃ δι' ὑπερβάλλουσαν δειλίαν καὶ ἀνανδρίαν, τὴν συνεχῆ τῆς χειρὸς ἐνόχλησιν οὐχ ὑφίσταται. Ἀλλὰ καὶ συνανθρωπιστικοί τινες τῶν ὀρνίθων εἰσὶ, τὰς αὐτὰς ἡμῖν οἰκήσεις καταδεχόμενοι· ἄλλοι δὲ ὄρειοι, καὶ φιλέρημοι. Μεγίστη δὲ διαφορὰ καὶ ἡ περὶ τὴν φωνὴν ἰδιότης ἑκάστου. Οἱ μὲν γὰρ κωτίλοι καὶ λάλοι τῶν ὀρνίθων εἰσίν· οἱ δὲ σιγηλοί. Καὶ τὰ μὲν ᾠδικὰ καὶ πολύφωνα· τὰ δὲ ἄμουσα παντελῶς καὶ ᾠδῆς ἄμοιρα. Καὶ τὰ μὲν μιμηλὰ, ἢ ἐκ φύσεως ἔχοντα τὸ μιμεῖσθαι, ἢ ἐξ ἀσκήσεως προσλαβόντα· τὰ δὲ μονό τροπον καὶ ἀμετάβλητον τὴν φωνὴν ἀφιέντα. Γαῦρον ὁ ἀλεκτρυών· φιλόκαλον ὁ ταώς· λάγνιοι αἱ περιστεραὶ καὶ αἱ κατοικίδιοι ὄρνεις, ἐπὶ παντὸς καιροῦ τὸ συνουσιαστικὸν ἔχουσαι. Δολερὸν ὁ πέρδιξ καὶ ζηλότυπον, κακούργως συμπράττων τοῖς θηραταῖς πρὸς τὴν ἄγραν. 8.4 Μυρίαι, ὡς ἔφαμεν, καὶ τῶν πράξεων καὶ τῶν βίων διαφοραί. Ἔστι δέ τινα καὶ πολιτικὰ τῶν ἀλόγων, εἴπερ πολιτείας ἴδιον, τὸ πρὸς ἓν πέρας κοινὸν συννεύειν τὴν ἐνέργειαν τῶν καθ' ἕκαστον, ὡς ἐπὶ τῶν μελισσῶν ἄν τις ἴδοι. Καὶ γὰρ ἐκείνων κοινὴ μὲν ἡ οἴκησις, κοινὴ δὲ ἡ πτῆσις, ἐργασία δὲ πάντων μία· καὶ τὸ μέγιστον, ὅτι ὑπὸ βασιλεῖ καὶ ταξιάρχῳ τινὶ τῶν ἔργων ἅπτονται, οὐ πρότερον καταδεχόμεναι ἐπὶ τοὺς λειμῶνας ἐλθεῖν, πρὶν ἂν ἴδωσι κατάρξαντα τὸν βασιλέα τῆς πτήσεως. Καὶ ἔστιν αὐταῖς οὐ χειροτονητὸς ὁ βασιλεὺς (πολλάκις γὰρ ἀκρισία δήμου τὸν χείριστον εἰς ἀρχὴν προεστήσατο), οὐδὲ κληρωτὴν ἔχων τὴν ἐξουσίαν (ἄλογοι γὰρ αἱ συντυχίαι τῶν κλήρων ἐπὶ τὸν πάντων ἔσχατον πολλάκις τὸ κράτος φέρουσαι), οὐδὲ ἐκ πατρικῆς διαδοχῆς τοῖς βασιλείοις ἐγκαθεζόμενος (καὶ γὰρ καὶ οὗτοι ἀπαίδευτοι καὶ ἀμαθεῖς πάσης ἀρετῆς, διὰ τρυφὴν καὶ κολακείαν, ὡς τὰ πολλὰ, γίνονται), ἀλλ' ἐκ φύσεως ἔχων τὸ κατὰ πάντων πρωτεῖον, καὶ μεγέθει δια φέρων καὶ σχήματι καὶ τῇ τοῦ ἤθους πραότητι.
thought_title: Kinds of birds and the polity of bees
orientation: Basil is still expounding the fifth day's creation of birds, now surveying differences among bird kinds and then turning to bees as an example of political order among irrational creatures.
pass_a_gloss: Now some have already attempted also to use name-makings, so that, just as through certain branding-irons of the unusual and strange naming, the peculiarity of each kind might be recognized. And some they named split-winged, as the eagles; others skin-winged, as the bats; others feathered, as the wasps; others sheath-winged, as the beetles, and as many as, born in certain cases and coverings, when their sheath burst around them, were set free for flight. But for us a sufficient marking for the peculiarity of the kinds is common usage, and the distinctions from Scripture concerning clean and unclean. One kind then is that of the flesh-eaters, and another equipment befitting the manner of their way of life, sharp points of claws, and a hooked lip, and a sharp wing, so that the prey may both be seized easily, and torn apart may become food for the captor. Another is the equipment of the seed-pickers; another of those fed from everything that happens along. And among these there are very many differences. For some of them are gregarious, except the predatory ones; and of these nothing is communal except the pairing according to mates. Countless others have chosen the gathered-together life, as doves, and cranes, and starlings, and jackdaws. Again among these some are without ruler and, as it were, self-governing; others accept being arranged under a leader, as the cranes. Now there is also another difference among these, according to which some are stay-at-home and native, while others are by nature to depart very far, and when winter draws near to move away for the most part. Tame and domesticated do many of the birds become when reared, except indeed the weak ones, which because of excessive timidity and cowardice do not endure the continual disturbance of the hand. But also some of the birds are human-companionable, accepting the same dwellings as we; others are mountain-dwelling and solitude-loving. A very great difference also is the peculiarity of each concerning voice. For some of the birds are chattering and talkative; others silent. And some are songful and many-voiced; others entirely unmusical and without share of song. And some are imitative, either having from nature the ability to imitate, or having acquired it from practice; others emit a single-mode and unchangeable voice. Proud is the rooster; beauty-loving the peacock; lustful are the doves and the domestic hens, having the mating impulse at every season. Deceitful is the partridge and jealous, wickedly cooperating with the hunters toward the capture. Countless, as we said, are the differences both of actions and of ways of life. And there are also some political ones among the irrational creatures, if indeed the mark of a polity is that the activity of each individual converges toward one common end, as one might see in the case of the bees. For also of those the dwelling is common, and the flight is common, and the work of all is one; and the greatest thing, that under a king and some commander they take hold of their works, not previously accepting to go to the meadows until they see the king begin the flight. And their king is not elected by vote (for often the poor judgment of the people has set the worst man into office), nor does he hold his authority by lot (for the chances of lots are irrational, often bringing the power to the very last of all), nor is he seated in the palace by paternal succession (for also these become uneducated and ignorant of all virtue, through luxury and flattery, for the most part), but having from nature the preeminence over all, and differing in size and in form and in the gentleness of his character.

pass_b_english: Some people have already tried to use name-makings, so that the distinctive character of each kind might be recognized through these unfamiliar and strange names, as if by branding marks. They called some split-winged, like the eagles; others skin-winged, like the bats; others feathered, like the wasps; others sheath-winged, like the beetles and all those that are born inside certain cases and coverings, and when their sheath breaks open they are set free for flight. But for us, common usage is a sufficient indication of the distinctiveness of the kinds, along with the distinctions in Scripture concerning clean and unclean creatures.

So one kind is that of the flesh-eaters, and their equipment is suited to their manner of life: sharp talons, a hooked beak, and a pointed wing, so that the prey can be seized easily and, once torn apart, become food for the one who caught it. The equipment of the seed-pickers is different; that of those that feed on whatever they happen to find is different again. And among these there are very many differences.

Some of them are gregarious, except for the predatory ones; none of these is social except for the pairing of mates. Countless others have chosen the life of the flock, like doves, cranes, starlings, and jackdaws. Again, among these some have no ruler and are, so to speak, self-governing; others accept being arranged under a leader, like the cranes. And there is yet another difference among them, according to which some are stay-at-home and native to a place, while others are by nature inclined to depart very far, and for the most part to move away when winter approaches.

Many birds, when raised by hand, become tame and domesticated—except, of course, the weak ones, which because of their excessive timidity and lack of spirit cannot endure the constant disturbance of the hand. But some birds are human-companionable, accepting the same dwellings as we do; others are mountain-dwellers and lovers of solitude. The greatest difference is also the distinctive character of each one's voice. Some birds are chatterers and talkative; others are silent. Some are songful and have many voices; others are entirely without music and have no share in song. Some are imitative, either having the ability to imitate by nature or acquiring it through practice; others send forth a voice of one single type, unchangeable.

The rooster is proud; the peacock is a lover of beauty; doves and domestic hens are lustful, having the impulse to mate at every season. The partridge is deceitful and jealous, working knavishly with the hunters toward the capture.

There are countless differences, as we said, in their activities and their ways of life. And there are even some political ones among the irrational creatures—if indeed the mark of a political community is that the activity of each individual converges toward one common end, as one might see in the case of the bees. For their dwelling is common, their flight is common, and the work of all is one; and what is greatest, they set about their tasks under a king and a commander of some sort, not consenting to go out to the meadows until they see the king take the lead in flight. And their king is not elected by vote—for often the poor judgment of the people has set the worst man in power—nor does he hold his authority by lot, for the chances of the lot are irrational and often bring power to the lowest of all; nor does he sit in the royal palace by paternal succession, for such kings also become uneducated and ignorant of every virtue, for the most part through luxury and flattery. Rather, he has his preeminence over all from nature, excelling in size and in form and in the gentleness of his character.

problems.quote: working wickedly with the hunters to help them catch their prey
problems.source_quote: κακούργως συμπράττων τοῖς θηραταῖς πρὸς τὴν ἄγραν
problems.why: The partridge's deceit works κακούργως ('knavishly, by trickery')—it uses decoy tactics to lure other partridges, not 'help the hunters.' The bird is victim, not accomplice.
problems.fix: working knavishly against its own kind for the hunters' catch
problems.ruling: συμπράττων τοῖς θηραταῖς = 'working with the hunters'; partridge deceives hunters, not helps them. Misleads reader.

edits.old: working wickedly with the hunters to help them catch their prey
edits.new: working knavishly with the hunters toward the capture

fixed: The source κακούργως συμπράττων τοῖς θηραταῖς πρὸς τὴν ἄγραν means the partridge acts knavishly in cooperation with the hunters toward the capture, not that it helps the hunters catch prey. The English 'to help them catch their prey' misstates the bird's role; changed to 'toward the capture' to match πρὸς τὴν ἄγραν.

last_rejected.why: σφῆκες are wasps, but context shows these are flying insects with feathers (πτιλωτὰ), so likely 'moths' or a feathery-winged insect; wasps are not feathered.
last_rejected.ruling: σφῆκας = wasps; πτιλωτά is the author's classification, correctly rendered. Not translator's job to fix ancient taxonomy.

last_rejected.why: αὐτόνομα means 'self-named' or 'having their own name/laws,' not 'self-governing' in the political sense; these birds lack a leader, not make laws.
last_rejected.ruling: αὐτόνομα metaphorically means 'self-governing'; context contrasts with having a leader. Standard rendering, not error.

last_rejected.why: ἐκτοπίζειν means 'to go into foreign/distant places,' not merely 'move away'; the contrast is between local and migratory birds.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐκτοπίζειν = 'move away/displace'; 'move away' is within normal range. Mere preference.

last_rejected.why: ἀσθενῶν here means 'delicate' or 'fragile' in temperament, not physically weak; the context is timidity, not frailty.
last_rejected.ruling: ἀσθενῶν = 'weak'; context explains timidity. 'Weak' is normal range, not error.

last_rejected.why: συνανθρωπιστικοί means 'accustomed to live with humans,' not merely 'companionable'; it's about cohabitation, not friendliness.
last_rejected.ruling: συνανθρωπιστικοί = 'human-companionable'; next clause 'same dwellings as we do' clarifies cohabitation. Adequate rendering.

last_rejected.why: πολιτικὰ here means 'living in a polis/city-state,' i.e., 'social' or 'communal' in the technical Greek sense, not 'political' in modern sense.
last_rejected.ruling: πολιτικὰ = 'political'; author defines it as communal convergence. 'Political' is standard and contextually clarified.

last_rejected.why: ταξιάρχῃ is a specific military rank, 'commander of a company/taxis,' not vague 'commander of some sort.'
last_rejected.ruling: ταξιάρχῳ τινὶ = 'commander of some sort'; τινὶ justifies 'of some sort'. Adequate rendering.

last_rejected.why: κατάρξαντα means 'begin' or 'initiate,' not 'take the lead in'; the king starts the flight, not leads it.
last_rejected.fix: see the king begin the flight
last_rejected.ruling: κατάρξαντα = 'take the lead/begin'; 'take the lead in flight' captures both senses. Not error.

last_rejected.why: ἔσχατον means 'last' or 'uttermost,' i.e., the most unfit, not 'lowest' in social class.
last_rejected.fix: the last of all or the most unfit
last_rejected.ruling: ἔσχατον = 'last/lowest'; 'lowest of all' is normal range. Not error.

last_rejected.why: The Greek says 'for these too become,' referring to hereditary kings; English 'such kings' blurs that this is a new category being dismissed.
last_rejected.ruling: οὗτοι = 'these/such'; 'such kings' correctly refers to hereditary kings. Not error.

last_rejected.why: The peacock's 'love of beauty' refers specifically to its display of tail feathers, a well-known trait; 'lover of beauty' loses the specific sense of self-adornment.
last_rejected.fix: the peacock loves its own beauty
last_rejected.ruling: φιλόκαλον = 'lover of beauty'; specific tail-display is reader's inference, not word's meaning. Not error.
